headline: Islamic-State Debate Returns as PAS Anchors PN State Governments in Northern Malaysia
context: PAS heads the Kelantan, Terengganu and Kedah governments; Bersatu took the Perlis MB post in Dec 2025. Bernama reported a 2024 Kelantan motion to re-enact provisions voided in Nik Elin, and a 2024 Kedah bill on its Syariah courts.

changes.summary: Correction: Replaced "PAS governs six states" with PAS governing Kelantan, Terengganu and Kedah and anchoring Perlis. Removed unverified survey figures (62%, 18%) and a 2021 Federal Court citation.

Correction: Replaced the claim that most Malay-Muslims reject both extremes with survey findings, including Pew in 2013. Named the Nik Elin (2024) ruling and Kelantan's move to re-enact the voided provisions.

Correction: Bersatu has held the Perlis MB post since 28 Dec 2025 and PAS took no exco posts; earlier editions said PAS anchors PN's Perlis government. Single-source religion claims are now attributed, and the court rulings are described as the court described them.

cards.big: PAS heads three northern state governments: Kelantan, Terengganu and Kedah. The Islamic-state debate is back on the agenda.
cards.sub: Bernama reported a March 2024 Kelantan assembly motion to re-enact the provisions the Federal Court voided in Nik Elin. The Federal Court polices the line.

cards.big: The Federal Constitution limits Shariah courts to State List matters, including family law and offences against the precepts of Islam.
cards.sub: Nik Elin (2024) voided Kelantan provisions touching federal criminal jurisdiction. The State List boundary is the controlling test.

cards.big: The Federal Court said Nik Elin had nothing to do with the position of Islam or the Shariah courts. It asked which legislature held the power.
cards.sub: The court upheld sections 13 and 30 of the Kelantan enactment because they fall within state power to control the spread of doctrine among Muslims.

cards.big: Polls on Islamic law in Malaysia turn on the question asked. Pew (2013) reported 86% of Malaysian Muslims it surveyed favoured sharia as official law.
cards.sub: Merdeka Center (2014) asked about readiness instead: 58% of its Malay respondents said Malaysia was not ready for hudud, and 30% said it was.

cards.big: The secular-versus-Islamic binary asks the wrong question. Polls that separate sharia in principle from hudud get different answers.
Like asking a country to choose between two rooms in a house that has 15. The binary framing erases the space where most positions actually sit.
cards.sub: The constitutional middle ground accommodates Shariah within the State List; the political question is whether any party builds a programme around it.

cards.big: The constitution already accommodates Islamic law within limits. The real debate is the scope of dual jurisdiction, and who decides where the line falls.
